sections.title: Nomenclature and classification
sections.text: Xerocomellus pruinatus (Fr.) Šutara is the name accepted by Index Fungorum; the combination was published in 2008. Its basionym is Boletus pruinatus Fr. (1835), and Xerocomus pruinatus (Fr.) Quél. is a historical name. It is a bolete in the family Boletaceae, order Boletales.

sections.title: Cap, pores and flesh
sections.text: The cap is usually 3–10 cm wide, dark brown to chestnut or purplish, often pruinose when young and then finely velvety; it cracks little, especially compared with X. chrysenteron. The fertile surface consists of tubes and pores, never gills: pores are yellow to olive-yellow, fairly broad and often angular with age. They may turn blue when bruised, but the intensity of this reaction varies among descriptions and specimens. The firm stem is yellow, often dotted or streaked with red, especially on its lower part; it has no net-like reticulation. The flesh is yellow and firm, with bluing that is generally weak or slow and sometimes most apparent near the stem base.

sections.title: Ecology and season
sections.text: This is an ectomycorrhizal species of mixed woodland, often associated with beech or oak; birch and conifers are also reported. It fruits mainly from late summer to autumn, with timing varying by region. Its known distribution is predominantly European.

sections.title: Edibility and caution
sections.text: The species appears in European mycological lists of recommended or edible mushrooms when sufficiently cooked. This does not identify an individual specimen: several similar boletes can be difficult to distinguish, and colour-change reactions vary. Do not eat a mushroom identified from this entry.

traits: Dark brown to chestnut or purplish cap, often pruinose when young and rarely cracked
Bolete with yellow to olive-yellow tubes and pores, fairly broad and often angular; no gills
Firm yellow stem, often dotted or streaked red, without reticulation
Yellow, firm flesh; bluing is usually weak or slow and varies
Ectomycorrhizal in mixed woodland, especially with beech and oak; fruits from late summer into autumn
safetyNote: Some lists include this species among edible mushrooms when sufficiently cooked. That depends on reliable identification; similar boletes can be hard to separate, and bluing reactions vary. Do not use this entry as a foraging or consumption guide.
